messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Kealani, a 63-year-old project manager with a reputation for meticulous planning, described the last eight months of her life as a "total system failure." The event itself was a blur, a chaotic rupture in an otherwise orderly existence. What started as a severe flu spiraled with terrifying speed into septic shock and a two-week stay in the intensive care unit. She has struggled to assemble a coherent narrative of that time, piecing it together from her husband’s strained accounts and her own fragmented sensory data. She doesn’t have words for what happened, only a collage of terrifying sensations: the relentless, high-pitched beeping of machines, the acrid smell of antiseptic, the brutal cold of the room, and the horrifying feeling of a tube down her throat, silencing her. When the memories surface, they are not thoughts but full-body invasions. Sitting at her desk trying to review a project timeline, she will suddenly feel the phantom pressure of the mattress against her back and the distinct, helpless weight of her arms, splayed and punctured by IV lines. It is so real that she feels her breath catch, her body reenacting its own past paralysis.

This visceral reliving has made her world a minefield. Her work, once a source of pride, is now a source of constant dread. She finds her concentration shattered, unable to follow the threads of a complex discussion in meetings or focus on the intricate details of a budget spreadsheet. More than once, her direct report has had to gently point out a glaring error she missed. At home, her husband, Lopeti, tries to be gentle, but his presence is often another trigger. If he touches her shoulder unexpectedly from behind, she flinches with a sharp gasp, a jolt of alarm that leaves them both shaken and silent. He has learned not to talk about friends’ health issues or even news reports about medical breakthroughs. Any conversation that veers toward illness causes Kealani to become intensely irritable, her voice sharpening as she shuts it down, a defensive anger that Lopeti struggles to understand. She knows it hurts him, but the alternative—letting the conversation continue—feels like inviting the hospital room back into her home.

Over the months, she has come to believe that her body is no longer her own; it is an unreliable and treacherous vessel that betrayed her without warning. This conviction has turned her into a relentless monitor of her own physical state, where every minor ache or flutter of fatigue is interpreted as a harbinger of another catastrophic failure. She feels a deep, corrosive shame about the scars left by the central lines and the profound weakness that lingers, a constant reminder of her body’s frailty. It feels, to her, like a personal failing. This profound distrust has led her to cancel three consecutive follow-up appointments with her cardiologist. The thought of walking into a medical facility, seeing the sterile equipment, the needles, the drips, and submitting to an examination feels less like a step toward health and more like a voluntary return to the scene of her own destruction.

The decision to seek therapy came after her manager suggested she take a leave of absence, citing her declining performance. The suggestion felt like a confirmation of her deepest fear: that the illness hadn't just nearly taken her life, but had succeeded in destroying it. The capable, confident woman who could manage multi-million dollar projects was gone, replaced by someone who was afraid of her own shadow and her own skin. Kealani arrived at her first session with a sense of quiet desperation, stating that she didn’t know who she was anymore. She hopes therapy can somehow give her back the life she lost, but she is terrified that the person she used to be is gone for good, and that all she has left is this broken, untrustworthy body and a future defined by fear.
